lines.text: Airplane windows are always round. Not for looks. Square ones once tore jets apart.
At cruising altitude, the cabin is pumped full of air, so the body of the plane swells like a balloon on every flight.
That stress flows through the metal skin, and around every hole, like water around a rock.
But a sharp corner squeezes the stress into one tiny point, several times higher than anywhere else.
In 1954, two de Havilland Comets, the world's first jet airliners, broke apart in mid air.
Investigators found fatigue cracks that grew, flight after flight, from the corner of a square cutout.
A rounded window lets the stress flow smoothly around it. No corner, no weak point.
And that tiny hole in your window? It makes the outer pane carry the pressure, and stops the glass from fogging up.
